newsitem.title: USA: Japan PM in U.S. amid fears of trade tension.
newsitem.headline: Japan PM in U.S. amid fears of trade tension.

text.p: Repeated warnings by U.S. officials on Japan's resurgent trade surplus could affect otherwise problem-free bilateral relations, Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said on Thursday.

"The first thing I want to find out when I arrive in Washington is whether President (Bill) Clinton will bring up specific trade issues," Hashimoto told reporters travelling with him from Tokyo to Washington.
But Hashimoto, who will also visit Australia and New Zealand, stressed that relations were good and trade was not expected to dominate the agenda.
"At the moment there are no major problems to solve between the two countries," he said.
Japanese officials said Hashimoto will meet Clinton on Friday and seek to reconfirm the relationship between the two countries toward and into the 21st century.

But some Japanese officials fear the United States will shift its diplomatic emphasis to trade issues now that strains over the U.S. troop presence in Japan have eased following the enactment last week of a law to extend the leases of U.S. military bases in Okinawa.

"I heard there are some opinions in the U.S. which are in favour of raising specific trade issues, but some people say it's not good to create an awkward feeling between us by putting those issues on the table," Hashimoto said.

Sandra Kristoff, director of Asian affairs at the National Security Council, told reporters this week that the trade deficit with Japan as well as with China "is something we are looking at very closely."
Japan's trade surplus with the United States rose 11.2 percent to $3.04 billion in March, the sixth consecutive month in which it had risen year-on-year.

Dissatisfied with slow growth in sales of American goods and services in Japan, Washington has been calling for progress in bilateral negotiations over such issues as automobiles, airline service, shipyards and telecommunications.
Japan wants the summit to be a venue for an exchange of opinions on world affairs such as the situation in the Korean peninsula and aid to poverty-stricken African nations.
"I want to discuss with President Clinton issues on which the two countries can work together," Hashimoto said.

He said he would thank Clinton for U.S. support for efforts to solve the hostage crisis in Lima, which ended on Tuesday when Peruvian troops stormed the rebel-held Japanese ambassador's residence and rescued all but one of 72 hostages held by leftist guerrillas. All 14 of the guerrillas, one hostage and two soldiers were killed.
"I am feeling very relaxed now because I don't have to ask the U.S. for more cooperation in ending the hostage crisis," he said.
Hashimoto is also expected to confirm with Clinton stepped-up efforts to conclude by the end of September an update of the 1978 joint "defense guidelines" for security copperation.
The U.S. wants firm assurances that U.S. forces could use bases in Japan for operations or transportation in case of a new war in Korea.

Asked how he will respond if Clinton urges Japan to join the United States and South Korea in providing food aid on humanitarian grounds to famine-stricken North Korea, Hashimoto sounded negative. "If North Korea wants humanitarian aid, they should be humane to Japan first."
Japan has held up a decision on the food aid because of public anger over allegations that North Korea kidnapped several Japanese citizens and brought them to Pyongyang.
